'''Biljana Plavšić''' ({{lang-sr-Cyrl|Биљана Плавшић}}; 7 July 1930 – 1 October 2026) was a [[Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina|Bosnian Serb]] politician, academic and scientist who served as [[President of Republika Srpska]] from 1996 to 1998. She also served as the [[List of Serb members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina|Serb member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina]] alongside [[Nikola Koljević]] from 1990 to 1992, and the first woman to reach this office. Plavšić was convicted of [[crimes against humanity]] for her role in the [[Bosnian War]]. Before entering politics, she taught biology at the [[University of Sarajevo]].<ref name="Martin-2000">{{Cite book|title=The almanac of women and minorities in world politics|url=https://archive.org/details/almanacofwomenmi0000mart|publisher=Boulder, Colorado: Westview Press|date=2000|isbn=978-0-8133-6805-4|first=Mart|last=Martin|pages=44–45}}</ref>

Plavšić was indicted in 2001 by the [[International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia]] (ICTY) for war crimes committed during the Bosnian War. She [[plea-bargain]]ed with the ICTY and was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2003, to be served in a [[Sweden|Swedish]] prison.<ref name=Traynor-27-10-2009>{{cite news|last1=Traynor|first1=Ian|title=Leading Bosnian Serb war criminal released from Swedish prison|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/oct/27/bosnian-serb-war-criminal-freed|access-date=30 December 2015|agency=The Guardian|date=27 October 2009}}</ref> She was released on 27 October 2009 after serving two-thirds of her sentence. Plavšić was, together with [[Radovan Karadžić]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Radovan Karadzic found guilty of genocide, sentenced to 40 years {{!}} CNN |date=24 March 2016 |website=[[CNN]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230531015347/https://www.cnn.com/2016/03/24/europe/karadzic-war-crimes-verdict/index.html |archive-date=31 May 2023 |url-status=live |url=https://www.cnn.com/2016/03/24/europe/karadzic-war-crimes-verdict/index.html}}</ref> the highest-ranking Bosnian Serb politician to be sentenced.

==Early life and academic career==
Plavšić was born on 7 July 1930 in [[Tuzla]], then part of the [[Kingdom of Yugoslavia]].<ref name="vreme1">{{cite news |title=Biljana Plavšić, the former president of Republika Srpska convicted in The Hague, has passed away |url=https://vreme.com/en/vesti/preminula-biljana-plavsic-bivsa-predsednica-republike-srpske-osudjena-u-hagu/ |access-date=5 October 2026 |work=[[Vreme]] |date=1 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="irishtimes">{{cite news |last1=Higgins |first1=Andrew |title=Biljana Plavsic, the only woman charged with war crimes in the Balkan wars, dies aged 96 |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/world/europe/2026/10/04/biljana-plavsic-the-only-woman-charged-with-war-crimes-in-the-balkan-wars-dies-aged-96/ |access-date=5 October 2026 |work=[[The Irish Times]] |date=4 October 2026}}</ref> She was the second child of a local high school biology professor and a housewife.<ref name="irishtimes" /> Her family moved to [[Sarajevo]] when she was four.<ref>{{cite book |author=Olivera Simić |title=Madam War Criminal: Biljana Plavsic, Serbia's Iron Lady |date=2025 |publisher=Hurst |isbn=9781805262862 |pages=45–46}}</ref><ref name="vreme1" /> As a child, she witnessed the execution of Serbs in the streets and lost relatives during the [[Ustaše]] purges following the Nazi occupation of Bosnia.<ref name="irishtimes" /> 

She got a degree in biology, was a university professor teaching biology at the [[University of Sarajevo]] and was elected the Dean of the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics in 1987.<ref name="vreme1" /><ref name="Martin-2000" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=27 October 2009 |title=Плавшићева стигла у Београд |work=[[Radio Television of Serbia|RTS]] |url=https://www.rts.rs/page/stories/ci/story/134/%D0%A5%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%B0/254651/%D0%9F%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%88%D0%B8%D1%9B%D0%B5%D0%B2%D0%B0+%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B8%D0%B3%D0%BB%D0%B0+%D1%83+%D0%91%D0%B5%D0%BE%D0%B3%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4.html}}</ref><ref name="irishtimes" /> She was a [[Fulbright Scholar]], and as such she spent two years at [[Boyce Thompson Institute for Plant Research|Boyce-Thompson]] institute at [[Cornell University]] in [[New York (state)|New York]] doing [[botany]] research, getting a PhD.<ref name="vreme1" /><ref name="irishtimes" /> She then specialized in [[Electron microscope|electron microscopy]] in [[London]], and [[plant virology]] in [[Prague]] and [[Bari]]. She published over one hundred scientific works and papers.<ref>{{Cite news |date=27 February 2003 |title=Biljana Plavsic: Serbian iron lady |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/1108604.stm}}</ref>

==Political career==
Plavšić was a member of the [[Serbian Democratic Party (Bosnia and Herzegovina)|Serb Democratic Party]] (SDS). She was the first female member of the [[Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina|Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina]],<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ahmetasevic |first1=Nidzara |title=Women Struggle to be Heard |url=https://iwpr.net/global-voices/women-struggle-be-heard |work=Institute for War and Peace Reporting |date=2 October 2002}}</ref> serving from 18 November 1990 until April 1992 after having been elected in the first multi-party elections in 1990 in [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro) |url=https://api.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/91/10503.pdf |page=114 |publisher=[[International Court of Justice]]}}</ref><ref name="initial">{{cite web |title=Prosecutor v. Biljana Plavšić: Initial Indictment |url=https://www.icty.org/x/cases/plavsic/ind/en/pla-ii000407e.pdf |publisher=[[International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia]] |id=Case No. IT-00-40-I |date=7 April 2000}}</ref><ref name="irishtimes" /> From 28 February 1992 to 12 May 1992, Plavšić became one of the two [[acting president]]s (alongside [[Nikola Koljević]]) of the self-proclaimed Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.<ref name="milosevic">{{cite web |title=Prosecutor v. Slobodan Milošević: Amended Indictment — Bosnia and Herzegovina |url=https://ictyoralhistory.sensecentar.org/files/Milosevic_Bosna_i_Hercegovina_Indictment_ENG_2002-11-22_ENG.pdf |publisher=International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia |id=Case No. IT-02-54 |page=4}}</ref> Thereafter she became one of two [[List of vice presidents of Republika Srpska|Vice-presidents of the Republika Srpska]]<ref name="milosevic" /> and from 30 November 1992 she was a member of the Supreme Command of the [[Army of Republika Srpska|armed forces of the Republika Srpska]].<ref name="initial" />

[[File:Biljana Plavsic (6938761997).jpg|thumb|Plavšić and other Bosnian Serb women leaders in [[Banja Luka]]]]

She declared that "six million Serbs can die so that the remaining six million can live in freedom" and considered the [[ethnic cleansing]] carried out against non-Serbs during the war to be a "natural phenomenon".<ref>{{cite book |last=Mann |first=Michael |title=The Dark Side of Democracy: Explaining Ethnic Cleansing |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-521-53854-1 |page=389 }}</ref> In July 1993, in a statement to ''[[Borba (newspaper)|Borba]]'', Plavšić reportedly claimed that Bosnian Serbs are ethnically-racially superior to [[Bosnian Muslims]] and claimed that:<ref>{{cite book |last=Wilmer |first=Franke |title=The Social Construction of Man, the State and War: Identity, Conflict, and Violence in Former Yugoslavia |publisher=Routledge |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-415-92963-9 |page=217 }}</ref>

<blockquote>Serbs in Bosnia, particularly in the border areas, have developed a keen ability to sense danger to the whole nation and have developed a defense mechanism. In my family they used to say that the Serbs in Bosnia were much better than Serbs in Serbia [...] and remember, the defense mechanism was not created through a short period of time; it take decades, centuries [...] I am a biologist and I know: most capable of adapting and surviving are those species that live close to other species from whom they are endangered.</blockquote>

In 1994, Plavšić stated that she and other Serbian nationalists were unable to negotiate with Bosniaks due to genetics:<ref name="ms">{{cite book |last=Shatzmiller |first=Maya |title=Islam and Bosnia: Conflict Resolution and Foreign Policy in Multi-Ethnic States |publisher=McGill-Queen's University Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-7735-2413-2 |page=58 }}</ref>

<blockquote>It was genetically deformed material that embraced Islam. And now, of course, with each successive generation it simply becomes concentrated. It gets worse and worse. It simply expresses itself and dictates their style of thinking, which is rooted in their genes. And through the centuries, the genes degraded further.</blockquote>

This statement by Plavšić was cited by Islamic studies scholar [[Michael Sells]] as an example of the pseudoscientific [[racial hygiene]].<ref name="ms" />

The [[Dayton Agreement]], signed in 1995, banned the then [[Politics of Republika Srpska#List of Presidents of Republika Srpska .281992-Present.29|President of Republika Srpska]] [[Radovan Karadžić]] from office and Plavšić was chosen to run as the SDS candidate for President of the Republika Srpska for a two-year mandate.<ref name="vreme1" /> She later got elected in the [[1996 Republika Srpska general election|1996 presidential election]].<ref name="irishtimes" />

[[Vojislav Šešelj]], at the [[Slobodan Milošević]] trial, described Karadžić's motives for nominating her.

<blockquote>She held very extremist positions during the war, insufferably extremist, even for me, and they bothered even me as a declared Serb nationalist. She brought [[Arkan]] and his [[Serb Volunteer Guard]] to Bijeljina, and she continued to visit him after their activities in [[Bijeljina]] and the surrounding area [...] Radovan Karadzic [...] believed her to be more extreme than himself in every way. He thought that the Western protagonists who tried eliminate him at any cost would have an even greater problem with her [...] Radovan Karadzic believed that she would continue to occupy her patriotic positions until the end. However, several months after she was elected, Biljana Plavsic changed her political orientation by 180 degrees under the influence of some Western protagonists and changed her policies completely.<ref>{{cite web|title=Vojislav Seselj Testimony|url=https://www.icty.org/x/cases/slobodan_milosevic/trans/en/050830IT.htm|publisher=International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia|date=30 August 2005}}</ref></blockquote>

Plavšić [[1997–1998 crisis in Republika Srpska|severed her ties with the SDS]] in 1997 and formed [[Serbian People's Alliance of the Republika Srpska|Srpski narodni savez]] (Serbian People's Alliance of the Republika Srpska), and nominated [[Milorad Dodik]], the then member of the [[National Assembly of the Republika Srpska]] whose [[Alliance of Independent Social Democrats|SNSD]] party had only two MPs, for Prime Minister.<ref name="vreme1" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hasić |first1=Jasmin |last2=Sijamija |first2=Elma |title=The Political Communication of Milorad Dodik |journal=Politička misao |volume=57 |issue=4 |year=2020 |page=80 |url=https://hrcak.srce.hr/en/file/367201}}</ref> As a candidate of the reform "Sloga" coalition, she lost the [[1998 Republika Srpska general election|1998 election]] to the joint candidate of the SDS and the [[Serbian Radical Party of the Republika Srpska]], [[Nikola Poplašen]].<ref name="vreme1" /><ref>{{cite report |title=Republika Srpska – Poplasen, Brcko and Kosovo |publisher=International Crisis Group |series=Balkans Report |number=62 |date=6 April 1999 |page=2 |url=https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/27976/062_republika_srpska.pdf}}</ref> During her time in prison, she released a book called "Witnessings" (Svjedočenja), revealing many aspects of the political life of the war-time Republika Srpska. In 1998, Plavšić conferred an honorary award on [[Momčilo Đujić]], a [[Chetnik]] commander who [[Collaboration with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy|collaborated]] extensively with the Italian and then the German occupying forces against the [[Communist Party of Yugoslavia|communist]]-led [[Yugoslav Partisans|Partisan]] insurgency.<ref>{{cite book|last=Bosworth |first=R.J.B.|title=The Oxford Handbook of Fascism|year=2009|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-929131-1|page=431}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Hoare|first=Marko Attila|title=Bosnian Serbs and Anti-Bosnian Serbs|url=http://www.bosnia.org.uk/bosrep/report_format.cfm?articleID=2803&reportid=125|newspaper=Bosnian Institute|access-date=27 November 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304042330/http://www.bosnia.org.uk/bosrep/report_format.cfm?articleID=2803&reportid=125|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2000 she resigned from the National Assembly and retired from politics.<ref name="vreme1" />

==ICTY sentence and release==
Plavšić was indicted by the [[International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia]] together with [[Momčilo Krajišnik]] and [[Radovan Karadžić]] for the "creation of impossible conditions of life, [[persecution]] and [[fear|terror]] tactics in order to encourage non-Serbs to leave the area, [[deportation]] of those reluctant to leave, and the [[liquidation]] of others". The Indictment charged Biljana Plavšić as follows:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.icty.org/x/cases/plavsic/tjug/en/pla-tj030227e.pdf|title=Prosecutor v. Biljana Plavšić judgement|publisher=International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia}}</ref>

* Two counts of genocide (Article 4 of the Statute of the Tribunal{{snd}} genocide; and/or, complicity to commit genocide)
* Five counts of [[crimes against humanity]] (Article 5 thereof{{snd}} extermination; murder; persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds; deportation; alternatively, inhumane acts)
* One count of violations of the laws or customs of war (Article 3 thereof{{snd}} murder)

She voluntarily surrendered to the ICTY on 10 January 2001, and was provisionally released on 6 September.<ref>{{cite web |title=Biljana Plavsic on Provisional Release |url=https://www.icty.org/en/press/biljana-plavsic-provisional-release |publisher=International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia |date=6 September 2001}}</ref>

On 16 December 2002, Plavšić plea bargained with the ICTY to enter a guilty plea to one count of [[crime against humanity|crimes against humanity]] for her part in directing the war and targeting civilians and expressed "full remorse" in exchange for prosecutors dropping seven other war crimes charges, including two counts of genocide. Plavšić's statement, read in her native [[Serbian language]], repeated her admission of guilt. It said she had refused to believe stories of atrocities against [[Bosniaks]] and [[Croats]] and accepted without question the claims that Serbs were fighting for survival.<ref>{{cite web |title=Statement of Guilt: Biljana Plavšić |url=https://www.icty.org/en/content/statement-guilt-biljana-plav%C5%A1i%C4%87 |publisher=International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia |date=17 December 2002 |access-date=2 October 2026}}</ref>

[[File:Biljana Plavšić (2021).jpg|thumb|238x238px|Plavšić in 2021 after recovering from [[COVID-19]]]]

In an interview Plavšić gave in March 2005 to the [[Banja Luka]] Alternativna Television, however, she admitted she had pleaded guilty because she could not prove her innocence, as she was unable to find witnesses who would testify on her behalf.<ref>{{cite news|title=Zatvorski dani B.Plavšić|url=http://www.b92.net/info/vesti/index.php?yyyy=2005&mm=03&dd=12&nav_category=64&nav_id=164146|newspaper=B92|date=12 March 2005}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Ne znam šta je s Mladićem, on ne bi nikada radio protiv Srba|url=http://arhiva.glas-javnosti.rs/arhiva/2005/03/13/srpski/P05031203.shtml|work=Glas javnosti|date=13 March 2005|language=Serbian}}</ref> She repeated this in an interview for Swedish ''[[Vi (magazine)|Vi]]'' magazine in January 2009.<ref name="Bosnian Institute">{{cite news|last=Goldberg|first=Daniel Uggelberg|title=Plavsic retracts war-crimes confession|url=http://www.bosnia.org.uk/news/news_body.cfm?newsid=2544|newspaper=Bosnian Institute|date=4 February 2009|access-date=16 May 2011|archive-date=19 March 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120319195058/http://www.bosnia.org.uk/news/news_body.cfm?newsid=2544|url-status=dead}}</ref> She claimed to have pleaded guilty in order to avoid the remaining charges against her, including genocide, and a long trial.<ref name="vreme1" /><ref name="Bosnian Institute"/> Her pleading guilty led [[the Hague]] tribunal to lower her sentence and drop the remaining charges.<ref name="Bosnian Institute"/> Plavšić would have likely have been sentenced to 20–25 years in prison if she had not pleaded guilty and all eight charges would have been taken into account.<ref name="Bosnian Institute"/>

Plavšić was sentenced to 11 years in prison. She served her sentence at the women's prison [[Hinseberg]] in [[Frövi]], [[Örebro County]], Sweden (since 26 June 2003). In December 2008, the Swedish [[Ministry of Justice (Sweden)|Ministry of Justice]] rejected a request for pardon by Plavšić. She had cited "advancing age, failing health and poor prison conditions" as the reasons for her request.<ref name="pardonplea">{{cite news |title=Sweden rejects Bosnian war crime pardon request |url=http://www.thelocal.se/16140/20081204/ |work=[[Agence France-Presse]] |publisher=TheLocal.se |date=4 December 2008 |access-date=6 December 2008 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081205121753/http://www.thelocal.se/16140/20081204/| archive-date= 5 December 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref> [[Željko Komšić]], a Croat member of the [[Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina]] had written a letter to the Swedish authorities in September 2008 urging them not to release Plavšić, stating that "any act of mercy would be big mistake and an insult to the victims and families of the victims".<ref name="pardonplea"/>

On 14 September 2009, [[Patrick Lipton Robinson|Patrick Robinson]], President of the [[United Nations]]' [[International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia]], told ''[[The New York Times]]'' that Plavšić "appears to have demonstrated substantial evidence of [[Rehabilitation (penology)|rehabilitation]]" and had accepted responsibility for her crimes. The Times added that "Under Swedish law, she becomes eligible for release 27 October, after serving two-thirds of her term, though her release date has not been set."<ref>{{cite news|title=Ex-Bosnian Leader May Be Freed Soon|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/09/16/world/europe/16briefs-bosnia.html|newspaper=New York Times|date=16 September 2009 | agency=Agence France-Presse}}</ref> She was released on 27 October 2009.<ref>{{cite news |title= Bosnian Serb 'Iron Lady' released |work=BBC News |date=27 October 2009 |url= https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/8327714.stm |access-date=27 October 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091029194527/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/8327714.stm| archive-date= 29 October 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref> On the same day, Milorad Dodik, Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, provided an RS government jet to pick up Plavšić and welcomed her to [[Belgrade]] after her early release from a Swedish prison.<ref name=balkaninsight>{{cite news|last=Barlovac|first=Bojana|title=Dodik Says Had Moral Reasons to Welcome Plavsic|url=https://www.balkaninsight.com/en/article/dodik-says-had-moral-reasons-to-welcome-plavsic|newspaper=Balkan Insight|date=28 October 2009}}</ref> Dodik cited "purely moral reasons" for doing so.<ref>{{cite news|title=Dodik speaks about welcoming Plavšić|url=http://www.b92.net/eng/news/politics-article.php?yyyy=2009&mm=10&dd=28&nav_id=62644|newspaper=B92|date=28 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100103015206/http://www.b92.net/eng/news/politics-article.php?yyyy=2009&mm=10&dd=28&nav_id=62644|archive-date=3 January 2010}}</ref> On 10 November 2009, Dodik revealed that he seriously considered giving Plavšić an office in the Senate. He stated "we are working on revising the law on the President of the Republic, which would award Plavšić, and other former presidents, the opportunity to enjoy some privileges like the office, monetary compensation, counselor, secretary, official car with a driver and so forth."<ref name=dalje>{{cite news|title=Dodik will give Plavsic office in the Senate?|url=http://dalje.com/en-world/dodik-will-give-plavsic-office-in-the-senate/281001|newspaper=Dalje|date=10 November 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020034745/http://dalje.com/en-world/dodik-will-give-plavsic-office-in-the-senate/281001|archive-date=20 October 2012}}</ref> 

After her release, Plavšić lived reclusively in Belgrade, where she died on 1 October 2026, at the age of 96.<ref name="bi">{{cite web |title=Bosnian Serb Wartime Leader Biljana Plavsic Dies Aged 96 |url=https://balkaninsight.com/2026/10/01/bosnian-serb-wartime-leader-biljana-plavsic-dies-aged-96/bi/ |website=Balkan Insight |date=1 October 2026}}</ref> On 7 October, Plavšić was buried in Banja Luka.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plavsic buried in Banja Luka, Dodik and Cavic speak |url=https://srpske.rs/en/news/svet/2026/10/07/biljana-plavsic-buried-banja-luka-banski-dvor-memorial |website=Srpske Novine |date=7 October 2026}}</ref>
